notes.text: Behold — And not only with the Jews, but all those who should be ingrafted into that Olive. It is not called the new covenant, because it was as to the substance new, for it was made with Abraham, Gen. xvii, 7, and with the Jews, Deut. xxvi, 17, 18, but because it was revealed after a new manner, more fully and particularly, plainly and clearly. Nor was the ceremonial law any part of it, as it was to the Jews, a strict observance of that. It was likewise new in regard of the efficacy of the spirit attending it, in a much fuller and larger manner.

Not according — The covenant which God made with the Jews when they came out of the land of Egypt, was on God's part the law which he gave them, with the promises annexed; on their part (which made it a formal covenant) their promise of obedience to it.

With — That is, with those who are Jews inwardly. And write it - The prophet's design is here to express the difference betwixt the law and the gospel. The first shews duty, the latter brings the grace of regeneration, by which the heart is changed, and enabled for duty. All under the time of the law that came to salvation, were saved by this new covenant; but this was not evidently exhibited; neither was the regenerating grace of God so common under the time of the law, as it hath been under the gospel.
I will forgive — God makes the root of all this grace to be the free pardon, and the remission of their sins.

glossa.text: *Behold the days.* By this testimony Paul, etc., *as far as* and that circumcision and the sabbath might be spiritually fulfilled.

*And he shall not teach.* That they may not seek Jewish masters and the commandments of men, but may be taught by the Holy Spirit, if indeed they shall have been the temple of God, and the Spirit of God shall have dwelt in them, who breathes where he wills, and has diverse graces: Yet the knowledge of the one God is the possession of all the virtues.

*For all shall know. ((HIER.))* Because all shall be etc., *as far as* not in the nature in which he lay hidden in himself even when he was seen.

notes.text: Thee only — Which is not to be, understood absolutely, because he had sinned against Bathsheba and Uriah, and many others; but comparatively. So the sense is, though I have sinned against my own conscience, and against others; yet nothing is more grievous to me, than that I have sinned against thee. Thy sight - With gross contempt of thee, whom I knew to be a spectator of my most secret actions. Justified - This will be the fruit of my sin, that whatsoever severities thou shalt use towards me, it will be no blemish to thy righteousness, but thy justice will be glorified by all men. Speakest - Hebrew. in thy words, in all thy threatenings denounced against me. Judgest - When thou dost execute thy sentence upon me.

Behold — Nor is this the only sin which I have reason to bewail before thee; for this filthy stream leads me to a corrupt fountain: and upon a review of my heart, I find, that this heinous crime, was the proper fruit of my vile nature, which, ever was, and still is ready to commit ten thousand sins, as occasion offers.

Truth — Uprightness of heart; and this may be added; as an aggravation of the sinfulness of original corruption, because it is contrary to the holy nature and will of God, which requires rectitude of heart: and, as an aggravation of his actual sin, that it was committed against that knowledge, which God had wrote in his heart.

Hyssop — As lepers, are by thy appointment purified by the use of hyssop and other things, so do thou cleanse me a leprous and polluted creature, by thy grace, and by that blood of Christ, which is signified by those ceremonial usages.
Joy — By thy spirit, seal the pardon of my sins on my conscience, which will fill me with joy. Rejoice - That my heart which hath been sorely wounded may be comforted.

Create — Work in me an holy frame of heart, whereby my inward filth may be purged away. Right - Hebrew. firm or constant, that my resolution may be fixed and unmoveable. Spirit - Temper or disposition of soul.

The joy — The comfortable sense of thy saving grace, promised and vouchsafed to me, both for my present and everlasting salvation. Free - Or, ingenuous, or liberal, or princely. Which he seems to oppose to his own base and illiberal and disingenuous and servile spirit, which he had discovered in his wicked practices: a spirit, which may free me from the bondage of sin, and enable me cheerfully to run the way of God's precepts.

glossa.text: *Unto the end, a psalm.* ((CASS.)) When Nathan rebuked him, the king did not blush to confess his sins publicly, etc., *as far as* what avails with God for the penitent. *Of David.* ((AUG.)) He is set forth as an example, not of falling, but of rising again if thou hast fallen, that thou despair not. ((CASS.)) The first thing is entreaty, etc., *as far as* full remission of sins is granted.

*Have mercy on me, O God. ((Ibid.))* This is a penitential psalm, etc., *as far as* because he foresaw that through this psalm many would perish. *According to thy great mercy.* Of a grave sin one would have to despair, were there not a great mercy *misericodia*. A great one cannot be defined, how great it is. *Great mercy. ((Ibid.))* A great mercy brought God down from heaven, etc., *as far as* when God is asked to pardon according to himself? *Of thy tender mercies,* etc. ((CASS.)) He asks through mercy and through tender mercy. And mercy is in the nature, tender mercy in the effect.

*Wash me yet more.* ((CASS.)) What manner of blotting out he would have, he adds: *Cleanse me,* etc. ((HIER.)) So wash that thou make clean; for certain things are washed which nevertheless are not pure.

*For iniquity.* ((AUG., CASS.)) Whose mercy he asks that he may pardon, because he knows him just, that he punishes sins, he adds: Punish thou not, because I punish. *For my iniquity,* etc. *Against me.* ((AUG.)) He had his sin behind his back, when the king gave sentence against the rich man who had seized the poor man's ewe, forgetful of himself.

*To thee only have I sinned.* ((HIER.)) For he alone punishes justly who has not in himself anything that may be reproved; and among men this is Christ alone. *To thee only.* ((CASS.)) Because a king is superior to all, he is to be punished by God alone. *Before thee.* Because he knows that he is everywhere; whence he accuses himself, because in his presence he did not blush to sin. *That thou mayest be justified,* etc. Whose words do not pass away, but are fulfilled. *And mayest overcome when thou art judged.* God is of such great justice *t antae*, etc., *as far as* that he may overcome as between himself and him, if they be judged.

*To thee only.* ((AUG.)) To Christ, who had no sin, etc., *as far as* in that he had so grievously offended God. *And mayest overcome.* ((AUG.)) Or, thou art so just that thou overcomest the devil, and death, and the Jews, when thou art judged: and in the judgment wherein thou wast judged.
*In iniquities.* ((CASS.)) The odium of the sin is lessened, etc., *as far as* he is accused of one and confesses all.

*For behold,* etc. ((AUG.)) He so gives mercy that he keeps truth, so that not even the sins of him whom he pardons are unpunished. For he pardons the man who punishes himself. Mercy therefore it is that a man is set free; truth, that the sin is punished. *Truth,* etc. ((CASS.)) Because in confessing he spoke the truth, which God seeks above sacrifices, he entreats that help be brought him. *The uncertain and hidden things.* ((AUG.)) There are hidden things also, in that to such men, etc., *as far as* whence he had the more to beware of sin. *The hidden things.* ((CASS.)) From the authority of him who makes them manifest, the confidence of washing and of being made white.

*Thou shalt sprinkle me.* ((CASS.)) The second thing is confidence in the mercy of God, which is very profitable: lest despair creep in, which is graver than all sins. *With hyssop. ((Ibid.))* Dipped in the blood of the victim, it was sprinkled over the body of the leper, signifying that the stains of sins are to be washed away by the blood of Christ. ((AUG.)) Hyssop is a lowly herb, etc., *as far as* in which there is a swelling, so humility, pride. *Above snow. ((Ibid.))* Incomparably: whence also on the mountain the garment of Christ shone as snow.
*To my hearing.* ((AUG.)) Mark the humble man. Let me hear thee, etc., *as far as* and because he is now humble, now *the bones that were humbled rejoice.*
*Turn away.* ((CASS.)) Made secure by that confidence, he asks the blotting out of all sins and a full restoration.

*In my bowels. ((Ibid.))* Whence the adultery went forth. In both parts, in soul and in body, he asks the remedy of healing, because in them he sinned. He so desires to be cleansed that he may be seen to wish to commit no such thing further.

notes.text: So also Christ glorified not himself to be an high priest — That is, did not take this honour to himself, but received it from him who said, Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee - Not, indeed, at the same time; for his generation was from eternity. Psalm ii, 7.
Psalm cx, 4.

The sum of the things treated of in the seventh and following chapters is contained, ver. 7-10; and in this sum is admirably comprised the process of his passion, with its inmost causes, in the very terms used by the evangelists. Who in the days of his flesh — Those two days, in particular, wherein his sufferings were at the height. Having offered up prayers and supplications - Thrice. With strong crying and tears - In the garden. To him that was able to save him from death - Which yet he endured, in obedience to the will of his Father. And being heard in that which he particularly feared - When the cup was offered him first, there was set before him that horrible image of a painful, shameful, accursed death, which moved him to pray conditionally against it: for, if he had desired it, his heavenly Father would have sent him more than twelve legions of angels to have delivered him. But what he most exceedingly feared was the weight of infinite justice; the being "bruised" and "put to grief" by the hand of God himself. Compared with this, everything else was a mere nothing; and yet, so greatly did he ever thirst to be obedient to the righteous will of his Father, and to "lay down" even "his life for the sheep," that he vehemently longed to be baptized with this baptism, Luke xii, 50. Indeed, his human nature needed the support of Omnipotence; and for this he sent up strong crying and tears: but, throughout his whole life, he showed that it was not the sufferings he was to undergo, but the dishonour that sin had done to so holy a God, that grieved his spotless soul. The consideration of its being the will of God tempered his fear, and afterwards swallowed it up; and he was heard not so that the cup should pass away, but so that he drank it without any fear.

Though he were a Son — This is interposed. lest any should be offended at all these instances of human weakness. In the garden, how frequently did he call God his Father! Matt. xxvi, 39, &c. And hence it most evidently appears that his being the Son of God did not arise merely from his resurrection. Yet learned he - The word learned, premised to the word suffered, elegantly shows how willingly he learned. He learned obedience, when be began to suffer; when he applied himself to drink that cup: obedience in suffering and dying.

And being perfected — By sufferings, chap. ii, 10; brought through all to glory. He became the author - The procuring and efficient cause. Of eternal salvation to all that obey him - By doing and suffering his whole will.

Called — The Greek word here properly signifies surnamed. His name is, "the Son of God." The Holy Ghost seems to have concealed who Melchisedec was, on purpose that he might be the more eminent type of Christ. This only we know, - that he was a priest, and king of Salem, or Jerusalem.

glossa.text: *He did not glorify himself.* The Son was glorified by the Father, when he said: *This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased ((Matth. III))*. Which glorification was foretold long before through the Prophet: *Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee ((Psal. II))*.

*Thou art a priest.* Now Christ is a priest, not according to that whereby he was born of the Father, God with God, coeternal with him that begat him: but on account of the flesh consumed, on account of the victim which he offered for us. *According to the order of Melchisedech,* who was not temporal, Scripture keeping silence as to the beginning and the end of his life, in a figure of Christ who lacks beginning and end. And as he offered in bread and wine and once, so also Christ under the species of bread and wine gave his body and his blood to the disciples.

*Prayers and supplications.* He speaks of the action and the life of Christ, whose every action is the instruction of the faithful, and a prayer to God. Whatever Christ did, they were prayers and supplications for all. The shedding of his blood was a mighty cry, in which he was heard, for the reverence of that same passion. The reverence is this, that being without sin he suffered for charity alone. *He was heard.* By this it is plain that through him we can obtain mercy, since he is now at the right hand of the Father.
*He learned,* etc. That is, he willingly took upon himself obedience even unto death.

*To all that obey him.* So greatly does the passion avail, that it suffices for all unto salvation, which salvation can well be through him, because he himself *is called,* etc. *He was made the cause of salvation,* not of any sort of salvation, but of eternal; nor to few, but to all; yet on this condition, that they obey him. For otherwise they will not be able to obtain salvation. And he himself can well be the cause of salvation to the rest, since *he was called by God a high priest,* as he also himself showed in very deed by his works that he was such. For because he fulfilled the office of a high priest, and was obedient to the Father in all things, and in himself came to so great a consummation of all good things that it sufficed even for the salvation of others, therefore *he was called by God a high priest,* and this, *according to the order of Melchisedech,* namely, that all the order of divinity might be considered in him which could be considered in Melchisedech.

notes.text: Certain Greeks — A prelude of the Gentile Church. That these were circumcised does not appear. But they came up on purpose to worship the God of Israel.

These came to Philip of Bethsaida in Galilee — Perhaps they used to lodge there, in their journey to Jerusalem. Or they might believe, a Galilean would be more ready to serve them herein, than a Jew. Sir - They spake to him, as to one they were little acquainted with. We would see Jesus - A modest request. They could scarce expect that he would now have time to talk with them.
The hour is come that the Son of man should be glorified — With the Father and in the sight of every creature. But he must suffer first.

Unless a grain of wheat die — The late resurrection of Lazarus gave our Lord a natural occasion of speaking on this subject. And agreeable to his infinite knowledge, he singles out, from among so many thousands of seeds, almost the only one that dies in the earth: and which therefore was an exceeding proper similitude, peculiarly adapted to the purpose for which he uses it. The like is not to be found in any other grain, except millet, and the large bean.
He that loveth his life — More than the will of God; shall lose it eternally: and he that hateth his life - In comparison of the will of God, shall preserve it. Matt. x, 39.
Let him follow me — By hating his life: and where I am - In heaven. If any man serve me - Thus, him will the Father honour.

Now is my soul troubled — He had various foretastes of his passion. And what shall I say? - Not what shall I choose? For his heart was fixed in choosing the will of his Father: but he laboured for utterance. The two following clauses, Save me from this hour - For this cause I came - Into the world; for the sake of this hour (of suffering) seem to have glanced through his mind in one moment. But human language could not so express it.
Father, glorify thy name — Whatever I suffer. Now the trouble was over. I have glorified it - By thy entrance into this hour. And I will glorify it - By thy passing through it.

The multitude who stood and heard — A sound, but not the distinct words - In the most glorious Revelations there may remain something obscure, to exercise our faith. Said, It thundered -Thunder did frequently attend a voice from heaven. Perhaps it did so now.

Now — This moment. And from this moment Christ thirsted more than ever, till his baptism was accomplished. Is the judgment of this world - That is, now is the judgment given concerning it, whose it shall be. Now shall the prince of this world - Satan, who had gained possession of it by sin and death, be cast out -That is, judged, condemned, cast out of his possession, and out of the bounds of Christ's kingdom.

Lifted up from the earth — This is a Hebraism which signifies dying. Death in general is all that is usually imported. But our Lord made use of this phrase, rather than others that were equivalent, because it so well suited the particular manner of his death. I will draw all men - Gentiles as well as Jews. And those who follow my drawings, Satan shall not be able to keep.

glossa.text: *These therefore came.* He shows the Gentiles converted through the preaching of the apostles.

*But Jesus.* They were of the Jews who cried out: *Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord;* now the Gentiles seek to see him: behold, two walls meeting. And so the corner stone speaks. *The hour is come that should be glorified.* This is not a glorification concerning those who wish to see him, but on their occasion he announces the coming fulness of the Gentiles, when he has been glorified in heaven. But this height of glorification is preceded by the lowliness of the passion; whence: *Amen, amen I say to you,* etc. Where he calls himself the grain which must be mortified and multiplied; to which passion, having now exhorted them, he adds: *He that loveth his life,* etc.

*Unless the grain of wheat. ((AUG.))* He himself is the wheat by which the faithful soul ought to live. The grain, from which the spiritual harvest ought to rise. Though there be many grains of seeds, he compares himself to none but wheat; whence the custom began in the Church that of this grain alone the body of the Lord is confected.

*He that loveth. ((AUG.))* He who loves in this life loses in the life to come what is more fitting; whence he adds: *He that hateth his life,* etc. He does not love but hates his life in this world who, loving God, chooses rather to be slain than to sin against him.

*If any man minister to me.* The price of the work by which he is ministered to is to be with him, without whom it is nowhere good to be, and with whom it is nowhere ill to be; whence he adds more openly, *if any man minister to me.*

*Now my soul is troubled. And what shall I say?* The passion having been foretold, and the exhortation to it set beneath it, as though the voice of his own fortitude had been given, he adds the affection of our infirmity, which he truly took upon himself, but of his will, for us, lest we despair of this infirmity: in which also he teaches what we ought to say, and whither to flee. As if he should say: My soul is troubled; what shall I say? whither shall I flee? whom shall I call upon? in whom shall I hope? In the Father who saves, to whom I set forth my will, because for this cause, that I might suffer these things, I came unto this hour; whence also my glorification comes about thus, and in my members.
*Father, glorify.* I seek salvation, but I do not refuse the passion; for which passion glorify me, which is the glory of thy name.
*This voice came not because of me.* He shows that this voice did not declare to him what he knew, but to those to whom it had to be declared.

*Now is the judgment.* Of discernment, namely, which is before the last judgment of damnation, because now, through the passion, the right of the devil being destroyed, many shall be set free; whence, expounding it, he subjoins: I suffer, I am troubled, and through these things, etc. *He shall be cast out.* He shall be driven out from the redeemed; when the apostles preach he shall be fully driven out, who of old by few, even though a man be tempted without, does not hurt within.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, ‘You are my son. Today I have become your father.’
echoes.note: Re-cited from 1:5, now welded to priesthood: the same divine ‘today’ that enthrones the Son also installs him as high priest. Recurrence binding the two halves of the letter together.

echoes.text: Yahweh has sworn, and will not change his mind: ‘You are a priest forever in the order of Melchizedek.’
echoes.note: The hinge of the whole letter. Ps 110:1 crowned the Son at 1:13; now verse 4 of the same psalm makes him priest — a priesthood older than Aaron's, sworn by an oath. Named here, expounded at length in chapter 7.

echoes.text: Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread and wine: and he was priest of God Most High.
echoes.note: The name ‘Melchizedek’ (vv. 6, 10) points beyond Ps 110:4 to its narrative root in Gen 14:18, the only other Old Testament Melchizedek text and the one ch. 7 will expound at length. The repeated naming is Hays' recurrence in advance — the figure is planted here and harvested in chapter 7.

echoes.text: For he has not despised nor abhorred the affliction of the afflicted, Neither has he hidden his face from him; but when he cried to him, he heard.
echoes.note: ‘Strong crying… having been heard for his godly fear’ (v. 7) reads the righteous sufferer's vindication: the very psalm of the cross (Ps 22, already cited at 2:12) testifies that God ‘heard’ the afflicted one's cry. Thematic coherence and recurrence of Ps 22 in Hebrews make this a heard, if unquoted, link to the Passion.

echoes.text: I love Yahweh, because he listens to my voice, and my cries for mercy. Because he has turned his ear to me, therefore I will call on him as long as I live. The cords of death surrounded me, the pains of Sheol got a hold of me. I found trouble and sorrow. Then I called on Yahweh’s name: “Yahweh, I beg you, deliver my soul.”
echoes.note: ‘Prayers and petitions… to him who was able to save him from death, and having been heard’ (v. 7) closely tracks the lament-deliverance pattern of Ps 116: encircled by the ‘cords of death,’ the petitioner cries and is heard. Scholars (Beale & Carson) hear the Gethsemane prayer voiced through the lament psalms; medium volume, strong thematic fit.

echoes.text: “Hear my prayer, Yahweh, and give ear to my cry. Don’t be silent at my tears. For I am a stranger with you, a foreigner, as all my fathers were.
echoes.note: ‘With strong crying and tears’ (v. 7) — the explicit ‘tears’ — faintly echoes the lament topos of Ps 39:12, where the sufferer begs God not to ‘be silent at my tears.’ Low verbal volume and a contested identification (any lament psalm could supply the motif), included for maximal coverage.

echoes.text: You shall not go out from the door of the Tent of Meeting for seven days, until the days of your consecration are fulfilled: for he shall consecrate you seven days.
echoes.note: ‘Having been made perfect’ (teleiōtheis, v. 9) carries the cultic sense of priestly ‘perfecting/consecration’ — the LXX teleioō word-group renders the ‘fill the hand’ ordination of Lev 8 (cf. 8:33, the seven-day consecration). A faint figural link: Christ's perfecting through suffering reworks the priest's installation rite. LXX-specific; invisible in the Hebrew ‘fill the hands.’

echoes.text: It shall happen in the latter days, that the mountain of Yahweh’s house shall be established on the top of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; and all nations shall flow to it. Many peoples shall go and say, “Come, let’s go up to the mountain of Yahweh, to the house of the God of Jacob; and he will teach us of his ways, and we will walk in his paths.” For out of Zion the law shall go out, and Yahweh’s word from Jerusalem.
echoes.note: The Greeks who 'went up to worship' and seek Jesus faintly enact the pilgrimage of the nations to Zion in the last days. Coherence with John's universalizing 'I will draw all people' (v.32) gives the motif some weight; low because no verbal contact.

echoes.text: In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening don’t withhold your hand; for you don’t know which will prosper, whether this or that, or whether they both will be equally good.
echoes.note: The seed-sowing wisdom of 'in the morning sow your seed... you do not know which will prosper' lies behind the grain-of-wheat agricultural maxim, though Jesus inverts it: the seed must die to bear fruit. Faint and generic; sowing imagery was broadly available.

echoes.text: Those who sow in tears will reap in joy. He who goes out weeping, carrying seed for sowing, will certainly come again with joy, carrying his sheaves.
echoes.note: 'Those who sow in tears... goes out weeping, bearing the seed... comes home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves' offers a death-to-harvest pattern resonant with the grain that dies to bear much fruit. Thematic Coherence only; no lexical anchor, hence low.

echoes.text: Yahweh said to Moses, “Make a fiery serpent, and set it on a pole. It shall happen, that everyone who is bitten, when he sees it, shall live.” Moses made a serpent of brass, and set it on the pole. If a serpent had bitten any man, when he looked at the serpent of brass, he lived.
echoes.note: 'If I am lifted up from the earth' (hypsotho) reactivates the bronze-serpent type John named in 3:14: the lifted-up serpent that gives life when looked upon prefigures the crucified-glorified Son of Man. High Coherence and Recurrence across John; the verb 'lifted up' is the load-bearing link to Moses' standard.

echoes.text: Behold, my servant shall deal wisely, he shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be very high.
echoes.note: John's distinctive fusion of 'lifted up' with 'glorified' tracks the LXX of the Servant Song: 'my servant shall be exalted (hypsothesetai) and glorified (doxasthesetai) exceedingly.' The pairing hypsoo + doxazo is rare and precise, giving strong Volume; John reads crucifixion as the Servant's exaltation.

echoes.text: My soul is also in great anguish. But you, Yahweh—how long? Return, Yahweh. Deliver my soul, and save me for your loving kindness’ sake.
echoes.note: 'Now my soul is troubled... save me from this time?' echoes the lament psalter, esp. Ps 6:3-4 'my soul is greatly troubled... save my life,' the Johannine analogue to the Synoptic Gethsemane. Coherence with the psalmist's troubled-soul-then-deliverance pattern is strong; medium since John gives no citation formula.

echoes.text: I will put hostility between you and the woman, and between your offspring and her offspring. He will bruise your head, and you will bruise his heel.”
echoes.note: 'Now the prince of this world will be cast out' faintly resonates with the protevangelium's defeat of the serpent. Low and contested; the casting-out of the ruler is more cosmic/apocalyptic than tied to any single verse.

lines: Unless a grain of wheat falls and dies, it stays alone.
But if it dies, it bears much fruit.
I will write my law upon their hearts, says the Lord.
Create in us clean hearts, O God.

We would see Jesus.

Come, let us follow him home. Amen.

lines: A single grain lies in the dark earth, and unless it falls and dies, it stays a single grain.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
But buried, broken open, it rises into a harvest, and this is how the Son will be glorified.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
God will write a new covenant on hearts of flesh, and remember our sin no more.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
Now the hour has come; lifted from the earth, he will draw the whole world to himself.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross.
So we say with the seekers at the festival: we would see Jesus. Come, let us follow.
We are pilgrims on the way to the cross. Amen.
